name: Speed (distance ÷ time)
description: Computes average speed as distance÷time, in km/h from distance in km and time in hours. It is the constant speed that would cover the distance in the given time.
notes: This gives average speed, not instantaneous speed. Keep units matched (km and hours give km/h); convert minutes to hours before entering.

name: Fuel economy
description: Computes fuel economy as distance÷fuel, giving the distance travelled per litre of fuel in km/L. A higher value means better efficiency.
notes: This is km per litre, which is the inverse of L/100km used in some regions; a higher number is better here. Fuel must be nonzero.

name: Pace to speed
description: Converts a running pace in minutes per kilometer into speed in kilometers per hour by dividing 60 by the pace.
notes: Pace must be entered as minutes per kilometer in decimal form (6.5, not 6:30). Pace and speed are inversely related, so a faster pace gives a higher speed.

name: Speed to pace
description: Converts a speed in kilometers per hour into a running pace in minutes per kilometer by dividing 60 by the speed.
notes: The result is a decimal number of minutes; 6.5 means 6 minutes 30 seconds, not 6 minutes 50 seconds. Speed and pace are inversely related.

name: Travel time
description: Calculates how long a journey takes by dividing the distance by the average speed, giving travel time in hours.
notes: Assumes a constant speed and no stops; distance and speed must use consistent units (km and km/h). The decimal result is in hours, not hours and minutes.

name: Trip Fuel Cost
description: Divides trip distance by fuel economy to get fuel used, then multiplies by the price per unit of fuel, giving the total fuel cost of the trip.
notes: Fuel economy must be expressed as distance per unit of fuel (e.g. km/L), matching the distance unit; if your figure is in L/100km, convert it first.

name: Distance to Horizon
description: Estimates the straight-line distance to the visible horizon from the observer's eye height and the Earth's radius. It follows from geometry as the square root of twice the radius times the eye height.
notes: Eye height and radius in meters, result in meters; ignores atmospheric refraction, which typically extends the true horizon somewhat. Valid when eye height is small versus radius.

name: Great-Circle Distance
description: Computes the shortest surface distance between two points on a sphere from their latitudes and longitudes using the spherical law of cosines. Multiplying the central angle by the Earth's radius gives the great-circle distance.
notes: All coordinates in radians and radius in kilometers. The law of cosines loses precision for very short distances; the haversine formula is more numerically stable there.

name: Average Speed over Two Legs
description: Computes the average speed of a trip made of two legs as total distance divided by total time.
notes: The result is not the simple mean of the two speeds; the slower leg counts for more because it takes longer.

name: Time Saved by Driving Faster
description: Computes the minutes saved over a distance by driving at a higher average speed.
notes: Average speeds are assumed constant; traffic, stops and speed limits usually make the real saving smaller.

name: Fuel Cost per Passenger
description: Computes each person's share of the fuel cost of a car trip shared equally.
notes: Only fuel is counted; tolls, parking and wear on the car are not included.

name: Electric Car Energy Cost for a Trip
description: Computes the electricity cost of driving an electric car over a distance from its consumption per 100 km.
notes: Charging losses are not included unless they are already in the consumption figure; public fast charging is often priced higher than home electricity.

name: Annual Fuel Saving from a More Efficient Car
description: Computes the yearly fuel cost saved by switching to a car with better fuel economy.
notes: Fuel economy is in km per litre (higher is better). The result is negative if the new car uses more fuel.

name: Break-even Distance: Electric versus Petrol Car

variables.label: Extra purchase cost of the electric car

description: Computes the distance after which the lower running cost of an electric car pays back its higher purchase price.
notes: Only energy costs are compared; maintenance, insurance, tax, subsidies and resale value are not included.

name: Trip Time with Breaks
description: Computes the total time of a trip as driving time plus the time spent on breaks.
notes: Many road-safety bodies recommend a break of at least 15 minutes every two hours of driving.

name: Following Distance from a Time Gap
description: Computes the distance to keep behind the vehicle in front for a chosen time gap, such as the two-second rule.
notes: The two-second rule is a common minimum on dry roads; a longer gap is advised in rain, fog or snow.

name: Naismith's Rule (Walking Time)
description: Estimates hill-walking time by Naismith's rule: one hour for every 5 km of distance plus one hour for every 600 m of ascent.
notes: The rule dates from 1892 and assumes a fit walker without rests; descents are not counted.

name: Tobler's Hiking Function
description: Estimates walking speed on a slope by Tobler's hiking function (1993); the fastest speed, 6 km/h, is on a gentle downhill slope of −0.05.
notes: The slope is a ratio (0.1 means 10 % uphill; a negative value is downhill). The formula describes footpaths; off-path speed is lower.

name: Taxi Fare (Flag Fall plus Distance)

variables.label: Distance included in the base fare

description: Computes a taxi fare made of a base fare that covers a first distance plus a charge per km after that.
notes: Many taxi meters charge in fixed steps of distance and also add time when the car is slow or stopped, so the real fare can differ.

name: Speed from Timing over a Known Distance
description: Computes a speed in km/h from the time taken to cover a measured distance in metres.
notes: The result is the average speed over the measured distance; a longer distance gives a more reliable value.

name: Road Gradient as an Angle
description: Converts a road gradient given as a percentage (rise per 100 of horizontal distance) into an angle in degrees.
notes: A 100 % gradient is 45°, not 90°. Road signs give the gradient as a percentage.

name: Bicycle Gear Development
description: Computes how far a bicycle moves for one turn of the pedals: the gear ratio times the wheel circumference.
notes: A 700×25C road wheel is about 2.105 m around. A larger value is a harder gear.

name: Cycling Speed from Cadence and Gear
description: Computes cycling speed from pedalling cadence, the chainring and sprocket sizes and the wheel circumference.
notes: Cadence is pedal turns per minute. Tyre pressure and load change the real circumference slightly.

name: Average Fuel Economy over Several Fill-ups
description: Computes average fuel economy over several tanks as total distance divided by total fuel.
notes: Fill the tank to full each time so that the fuel added equals the fuel used. Averaging the economy of each tank would give a slightly different, less accurate figure.

name: Driving Range on the Fuel Left
description: Computes how far a car can go on the fuel left in its tank.
notes: Fuel gauges are not exact near empty; keep a reserve.
